topics.title: Teaching, Learning Theories & the Three Domains
topics.summary: Choose teaching methods that fit the learning goal, then check knowledge, attitudes, and skills with the right kind of evidence.
objectives: You can tell the difference between teaching activity and proof of learning.
You can compare adult, behaviorist, social, cognitive, and constructivist learning ideas.
You can sort a goal into the cognitive, affective, or psychomotor domain.
You can match each domain with the right way to evaluate it.
You can use learning preferences without treating them as limits.
You can recognize when you need more training before teaching.
topics.bigPicture:
Teaching is a process that uses planned strategies and approaches to change behavior. Learning is the outcome. It occurs within the learner, and you see it as an observable, measurable change in behavior. Handing over a leaflet is teaching activity. It is not proof that learning happened.

Nurses teach patients, families, staff, and students, and they keep learning, too. A good plan links the need, the goal, the method, practice, feedback, and evaluation. Learning theories give you tools, but the client’s actual response tells you if the plan works.
recap: Teaching is a planned process to change behavior. Learning shows as an observable, measurable change in behavior.
Cognitive means thinking. Affective means feeling. Psychomotor means skill.
Each domain needs its own evidence: teach-back, discussion of values, or return demonstration.
Knowing does not prove doing, and doing does not prove willing. Check each one.
Adults learn best when teaching is relevant and builds on their experience.
Good reinforcement names the exact correct action right after it happens.
Use learning preferences flexibly. A “visual learner” label is not a limit.
Get current training before teaching an unfamiliar device. Never improvise.

keyTerms.def: A process that uses planned strategies and approaches with the goal of changing behavior.
An outcome that occurs after exposure to information that adds to knowledge and skill. It shows as an observable, measurable change in behavior.
The “thinking” domain: knowing, understanding, and using information.
The “feeling” domain: values, attitudes, and willingness to act.
The “skill” domain: physical skills done with coordinated movement, such as using an inhaler or crutches.
An approach that stresses relevance, life experience, self-direction, and practical need.
A consequence after a response that makes it more (positive) or less likely to happen again. Your course stresses positive reinforcement, such as praise.
Showing a skill so the learner can watch and copy it. It is central to social learning.
The learner performs the taught skill while the nurse watches and evaluates it.
The ability to tell apart one’s own thoughts and feelings, recognize others’, and use emotions wisely in decisions.

sections.heading: What are teaching and learning?
sections.keyIdea: Teaching is a planned process aimed at changing behavior. Learning is the outcome, shown by a change in behavior you can observe and measure.
sections.body:
Your course defines the two terms this way. Teaching is a process that uses planned strategies and approaches. Its goal is to change behavior. Learning is an outcome. It occurs after a person is exposed to information that adds to their knowledge and skill.

The evidence of learning is a change in behavior. It can be observed and measured. It also becomes part of the person’s routine activities. Teaching shares information and skills to influence attitudes, perceptions, values, and behaviors.

So handing over a leaflet is teaching activity. A signed education form does not prove learning either. You control how you prepare and teach. You do not control what happens inside the learner.

Your course lists six attributes of learning. Learning:
bullets: Occurs within the learner.
Is the discovery of personal meaning and relevance of ideas.
Is a consequence of experience.
Is a collaborative and cooperative process.
Is an evolutionary process that builds on past learning and experiences.
Is both an intellectual and an emotional process.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 3–4

sections.heading: Nurses as teachers and learners
sections.keyIdea: Teaching is an expected part of nursing care. Nurses must also keep learning to stay current.
sections.body:
Nurses teach, and nurses keep learning. The table sums up what your course says about each role.

Nurses should also know their own strengths and their limits on a topic or skill. Knowing a concept does not make you competent with every related device. If you are unsure, get current, accurate training from a proper resource or colleague. Do not improvise. Errors you teach can become errors the client repeats at home.

rows: Teaching is an expectation of the nurse when giving care. The main focus is the patient and family.
How to give medications. Which symptoms should prompt a call to a healthcare provider. Therapies or treatments.
Other nurses and staff in healthcare settings. Students in academic settings.
Different agencies monitor how nurses teach patients, families, and other healthcare professionals.
A science-based education is the foundation of nursing. Nurses stay current with treatments and care through continuing education.
Impromptu and formal programs supported by employers. Advanced degrees, proving competency, and becoming credentialed. Programs on changes in regulations and requirements.

sections.example: A nurse must teach a client to use a home infusion pump model the nurse has never used. Discharge is tomorrow afternoon. First, the nurse gets current instruction on this pump from an appropriate resource, per policy. There is still time to teach before discharge.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 5–6 and 8

sections.heading: What makes teaching effective?
sections.keyIdea: Effective teaching follows planned steps, captures attention, involves the learner, and fits the learner’s age, condition, and abilities.
sections.body:
Effective teaching follows a series of planned steps. The goal is a change in behavior, such as learning a skill or understanding a topic. Your course calls the ability to capture the learner’s attention the “art” of teaching.

Support and encourage the learner to take part. Invite them to ask questions and seek clarification.

Teaching and learning also link to six related concepts in your course, shown in the table.

Your course lists ten characteristics of effective teaching. Effective teaching:
bullets: Identifies the learner’s preferred learning styles.
Uses several methods of teaching.
Asks the learner to identify areas of major interest.
Involves the learner in the learning process.
Is appropriate for the learner’s age, condition, and abilities.
Sets realistic goals that help the learner meet objectives.
Uses accurate, current, evidence-based information from reliable sources.
Helps the learner believe that learning is possible and likely.
Supports the learner with optimistic, positive reinforcement and feedback.
Is cost-effective.

rows: Teaching depends on clear two-way communication.
Culture and language shape how a person learns.
Teaching must fit the learner’s developmental level.
Teaching supports health and helps manage illness.
Diet is a common teaching topic.
Teaching prevents injury and errors at home.

sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 7–9

sections.heading: How do adults learn best?
sections.keyIdea: Tell adults why it matters, treat them as self-directed, and build on what they already know.
sections.body:
Your course says adult learners differ from child learners. Adults:

What the nurse does: communicate how and why the information is important and useful. Identify the learner’s past experiences. Help them fit the new information with those experiences.

Age alone does not guarantee readiness. Acute illness, cognitive impairment, new technology, or stress can mean an adult needs more support. Correct misunderstandings respectfully.
bullets: Need to know why they should learn something.
Prefer to be treated as capable of self-direction.
Have built up experiences that can enhance current learning.
Are often ready to learn what they must know to take care of themselves.
Bring a time perspective: they usually want to use what they learn soon.
sections.example: An adult asks, “Why do I need to learn this new routine when I already manage one at home?” A good first reply: “How have you been doing it at home? Let’s see what carries over and what is different.” This shows strengths and habits that may need changing.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 11

sections.heading: What do the other learning theories say?
sections.keyIdea: Each theory gives you a different tool. Know each one’s focus and limits, then pick what fits this patient.
sections.body:
Besides adult learning, your course covers four theories. Nurses must understand the focus and limits of each. Then select the theory or theories that best fit the specific patient.

Two constructivist terms: assimilation means fitting a new experience into what you already know. Accommodation means changing what you know to fit the new experience.

Most good teaching blends theories: explain why, show how, let the client practice, and give feedback. Watching alone is not enough when the client must do a skill alone.

rows: Learning occurs when a response to a stimulus is positively or negatively reinforced. Change behavior by changing the stimulus or what happens after the response.
Give praise or encouragement with each attempt or at each phase. Allow enough time to practice. Consider what in the environment affects learning.
Three mental processes: acquiring, processing, and using information. They can happen in order or at the same time. Learning occurs in three domains.
Fit strategies to the learner’s style and preferences. Assess developmental stage and emotional readiness. Adapt to the learner’s level. Choose objectives in all three domains.
Learning is a developmental process built from a person’s own experiences. Knowledge grows by assimilation and accommodation. Cooperative learning and problem solving help.
Acknowledge the learner’s prior learning experiences and build on them. Encourage the learner to engage with the nurse and others.
Learning comes mainly from instruction and observation. It focuses on imitation and modeling. Beliefs, perceptions, and thinking skills shape how a person interacts with the environment.
Model the skill. Ask for repeat demonstrations until performance is satisfactory.

sections.example: A client practicing with a walker moves it forward, then steps into it, as taught. Behaviorist reinforcement sounds like: “You moved the walker first, then stepped in. That keeps you steady.” General praise like “Great job!” gives nothing specific to repeat.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 12–15 and 17

sections.heading: What are the three learning domains?
sections.keyIdea: Cognitive is thinking, affective is feeling, and psychomotor is skill. Each needs its own goal and its own evidence.
sections.body:
Cognitive theory says learning occurs across three domains. Your course names them by what they involve:

Cognitive (“thinking”) goals are about what the person knows or can reason through. Affective (“feeling”) goals are about values, attitudes, and willingness. Psychomotor (“skill”) goals are about physical skill. A simple test: if the learner must physically do it, it is psychomotor.

One learning need can involve all three. A person may explain a technique but lack the dexterity to do it. Another may do it with coaching but refuse to use it at home. Do not treat one success as proof of the others. The “best evidence” column is added for the NCLEX.

rows: Name a concern and a personally valued goal.
Discussion and expressed choices over time.

sections.example: A client on new home oxygen explains why it is needed and sets up the equipment without prompting. Then the client says, “I am not wearing that tubing where my coworkers can see it.” Cognitive and psychomotor goals are met. The affective concern still needs exploring.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 13; evidence column added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: Do intelligence types and learning styles matter?
sections.keyIdea: Intelligence is not fixed or measured by IQ alone. Use each learner’s strengths and preferences as supports, not limits.
sections.body:
Your course presents two theories that challenge the idea that intelligence is static and based only on IQ. They help you notice each learner’s strengths. Intelligence levels are unique to each person. A person can function at a higher level in some intelligences than in others.

Effective teaching also identifies the learner’s preferred learning styles. Use them as supports, not limits. A “visual learner” can still learn from explanation and practice. Match methods to the task, too, and check the results.

Mix methods. An explanation gives the reason. A demonstration shows the movement. Practice builds the skill.

Know your own learning style. It can help you plan. But do not assume everyone learns the way you do.

rows: Based on how a stroke can damage one brain area while others stay intact. Intelligence has eight dimensions.
Linguistic. Musical/rhythmic. Spatial. Body/kinesthetic/movement. Personal. Symbols as intellectual strengths. Naturalist.
Added to the original seven. It means recognizing elements and patterns in the environment.
Measures the ability to tell apart one’s own thoughts and feelings, recognize others’ thoughts and feelings, and use emotions wisely in decisions.
It is as relevant to learning and success as IQ, or even more so.

sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 9, 16–17, and 22

sections.heading: How do I build a teaching sequence?
sections.keyIdea: Line up the need, goal, method, practice, and evaluation, and change the method if learning fails.
sections.body:
Start with the need and the behavior that matters most. If the outcome is not met, change the explanation, method, timing, or support. Repeating the same words louder is not a revision.

Present information from simple to complex. Keep essential content focused. Someone with a new diagnosis may need safety actions first and details later.

Learning develops over time. Document what the learner could do and what remains, not just the materials given.
steps: Identify the need and what the learner already understands.
Choose an observable objective and its domain.
Address readiness and access.
Teach in manageable steps.
Invite practice or application, and give feedback.
Evaluate and revise.
sections.example: A client newly diagnosed with heart failure says, “There is so much to learn that I can’t keep any of it straight.” Cognitive principles apply: organize the content, teach the most essential points first in small chunks, and build from there.
sections.source: Added: teaching sequence based on Teaching and Learning slides 8–9, 13, and 18

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Wrong answers treat teaching as learning, or one domain as proof of another.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: “Brochure given” is teaching. “Client demonstrated correctly” is learning.
A correct explanation does not prove safe performance. Watch a return demonstration.
Correct skill does not mean the client will use it. Explore feelings and values.
“You moved the walker first” reinforces. “Great job” does not say what to repeat.
Seeing a demonstration or video is not the same as doing it.
A picture preference adds pictures. It does not remove practice or explanation.
Experience with one model does not make you competent on another.

sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials (reviews slides 3, 9, and 12–15)

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Match the evidence to the domain, and choose the option that shows learning, not just teaching.
sections.body:
Expect items asking which domain a goal belongs to. Others ask which finding shows learning occurred. Select-all items may pair goals with evaluation methods.

Sample question: A client being taught crutch walking describes the gait correctly. During return demonstration, the client rests body weight on the crutch pads under the arms. What should the nurse do first?

A: Document that the client described the gait correctly.
B: Stop the client, coach weight bearing through the hands, and observe again.
C: Give a picture of correct posture to review later.
D: Praise the effort and review hand position at follow-up.
steps: Read the stem: knowledge is correct, but the skill is being done unsafely right now.
What is it really asking? How do you respond to an unsafe return demonstration?
Key cues: weight on the pads under the arms puts pressure on the nerves in the armpit and can cause injury.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A records knowledge but ignores unsafe doing. C and D delay the fix while the risk continues.
The answer: B. Stop, give specific correction, and watch the skill again.
Strategy: If the stem shows an unsafe skill, correct it now and re-observe. Saying it right is not doing it right.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials

sections.heading: Worked case: three domains in one routine
sections.keyIdea: One routine can have a knowing need, a feeling need, and a doing need at the same time.
sections.body:
A client can explain why a new device is prescribed. But the client does not want others to see it. The client also cannot complete one movement needed to use it.

Calling this one general “knowledge deficit” would miss two needs. The explanation shows cognitive understanding. The worry about being seen is affective.

The missed movement is psychomotor. A longer lecture fixes neither.
steps: Name each need: cognitive (met), affective (worry about being seen), psychomotor (one movement missing).
Connect the plan to the client’s own goals and experience.
Discuss the social worry without dismissing it.
Demonstrate the movement, and let the client practice with specific feedback.
Adapt the equipment or get help if physical ability limits the movement.
Evaluate each domain on its own. Document the evidence and plan reinforcement.

check.q: Why can a correct explanation exist alongside unsafe performance at home?
check.a: The cognitive goal may be met while physical ability, sequencing, willingness, or resources fall short. Each needs its own evaluation.

sections.source: Added: worked example based on Teaching and Learning slides 11, 13, and 15

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.keyIdea: This topic follows Module 41 slides 2–17 and 22. The notes below mark what the site adds.
sections.body: This lesson follows your Module 41 slides, “The Concept of Teaching and Learning.”
bullets: Definitions and attributes of learning: slides 3–4.
Nurses as teachers and learners, related concepts, and effective teaching: slides 5–9.
Adult, behaviorist, cognitive, constructivist, and social learning theories: slides 11–15.
Multiple intelligences and emotional intelligence: slides 16–17.

Course vs. current practice: your course lists “identifies preferred learning styles” as effective teaching. Current evidence does not show that teaching only to one style improves learning. Use preferences flexibly and verify learning.
Added for the NCLEX: the evidence column for each domain, the traps table, the sample question, and the worked case.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 2–17 and 22 (map of this topic)

mnemonics.name: Head, Heart, Hands
mnemonics.text: Head = cognitive (knowing). Heart = affective (feeling and willingness). Hands = psychomotor (doing a skill).

pearls: Teaching activity and evidence of learning are different things.
Knowledge, willingness, and skill must each be assessed.
For a skill, demonstration should be followed by learner practice.
Effective reinforcement names the exact correct behavior right after it happens.
Pick documentation that shows what the client explained or did, not what was handed out.
redFlags: Do not assume a client can do a safety-critical skill because they watched a video.
An unfamiliar or changed procedure needs accurate, current instruction before you teach it.
An unsafe return demonstration needs immediate correction, not a note for next visit.

checks.q: Which domain is tested when a client demonstrates a technique?
A client accurately describes a procedure. Does that prove safe performance?
checks.a: No. Watch a return demonstration and assess physical ability.

checks.q: How does adult learning shape the start of a teaching session?
checks.a: Explain why it matters, ask about the client’s experience, and involve them in setting goals.

checks.q: What is stronger evidence than “brochure provided”?
checks.a: A documented explanation, real-life decision, or demonstrated skill that meets the stated objective.
Any objective where the client physically does a step, such as priming the pen or injecting. Evaluate them by return demonstration.

topics.title: Assess, Plan, Teach & Verify Learning
topics.summary: Find the real learning need, remove barriers, set measurable goals, and use teach-back or return demonstration to guide reteaching.
objectives: You can assess readiness, motivation, literacy, language, physical ability, and resources.
You can write an observable, learner-centered objective.
You can use teach-back and return demonstration without blame.
You can find the real barrier before calling a client “noncompliant.”
You can document teaching evidence and flag unsafe gaps before discharge.
topics.bigPicture:
A teaching plan starts with assessment, not a stack of handouts. What must the client do? What do they already know? What will make learning possible today? The answers shape your content, timing, method, and support.

Learning shows in the client’s own explanation, decisions, or performance. Teach-back and return demonstration reveal mistakes while you still have time to fix them. A mistake is information about your teaching and the client’s needs. It is not proof the client failed.
recap: Assess first: what the client knows, must do, and has at home.
Motivated is not the same as ready. Pain, nausea, or exhaustion block learning.
Use plain language and teach-back with every client. Do not guess literacy.
Use a qualified interpreter for teaching, even if a bilingual family member offers.
Good objectives name an observable action and when it will be checked.
Teach-back checks your explanation. Return demonstration checks the skill.
After a teach-back error, reteach that gap a different way, then check again.
Missed doses or refills? Ask why. Cost, side effects, or access may be the real barrier.

keyTerms.def: An identified deficit in knowledge, information, or skills needed to achieve a particular goal.
The client’s current physical, emotional, and practical ability to take part in learning.
How important the client feels the learning is, and how much they want to learn and act.
How well a person can find, understand, and use health information to make decisions.
Asking the client to explain information in their own words, to check how clearly the nurse explained it. Added from current practice (AHRQ).
The client performs the skill while the nurse watches. Repeat until performance is satisfactory.
The extent to which a person’s behavior coincides with medical or health advice.
Attachment to a prescribed regimen. The patient is a committed, active participant and, by mutual agreement, helps choose the treatment.
A goal that states what the learner will explain, choose, or perform, and when it will be checked.

sections.heading: What do I assess before teaching?
sections.keyIdea: Start by finding the learning need: the gap in knowledge, information, or skills that blocks the client’s goal.
sections.body:
Your course defines a learning need as an identified deficit in knowledge, information, or skills needed to reach a particular goal. Find it before you choose a method.

Ask what the client knows, what worries them, and what they must do at home. A correct fact can sit next to a dangerous misbelief. “Tell me how you plan to take this” reveals more than “You know how, right?”

A knowledge gap is different from missing supplies or weak hands. Teaching fixes understanding. Other barriers may need equipment, a different plan, or caregiver help.
bullets: Knowledge: prior experience, usual routines, and misbeliefs.
Ability: can they see labels, open containers, coordinate movements, and remember steps?
Language and culture: native language, education level, and cultural influences.
Motivation and demands: desire to learn, personal demands, and responsibilities.
Home and support: home environment, support system, supplies, money, and transportation.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 10, 19, 22, and 25

sections.heading: What helps or blocks learning?
sections.keyIdea: Some factors make learning easier and others block it. A client can want to learn and still be too sick or upset to learn now.
sections.body:
Your course lists factors that help learning and factors that block it. Check both before you teach.

Motivation is wanting to learn. Readiness is being able to learn right now. A motivated client may be too nauseated or distressed to focus. Neither problem makes the client “uncooperative.”

Manage symptoms first. Pick a quieter time and place when you can. If a safety need cannot wait, give brief essential information now and return later. Depending on the type of teaching, the client may need a support person present.

rows: Cultural factors, such as native language
Information that moves from simple to complex
Psychomotor ability: muscle strength, motor coordination, energy
Repetition of key concepts and facts
Sensory acuity, such as vision and hearing

sections.example: A client wants to learn wound care but is nauseated, exhausted, and in severe pain. Staff are providing the needed care. First, the nurse addresses comfort. A longer practice session waits until the client can focus and move.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 18–19

sections.heading: How do I handle literacy and language?
sections.keyIdea: Give verbal teaching plus written materials in the client’s language. Use plain language and teach-back for everyone.
sections.body:
Your course lists native language as a cultural factor that can block learning. It calls for verbal information as well as written teaching materials. Written materials support the conversation. They do not replace it.

Use plain language and explain unfamiliar terms. Teach in small chunks, essential actions first. Do not guess literacy from looks, education, or job. A highly educated client may struggle with health words under stress.

“What questions do you have?” invites more than a rushed “Any questions?” When the client needs another language, use a qualified interpreter. A bilingual family member can support but should not replace one.
sections.example: A client says, “I left my reading glasses at home. Can you just tell me what it says?” The nurse explains the key points in plain language, then asks the client to explain them back. The nurse does not chart a literacy problem.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 19; plain language and interpreter use added (current standard)

sections.heading: How do I write a measurable goal?
sections.keyIdea: A strong objective names an observable action and when you will check it. Set realistic goals with the client.
sections.body:
Your course says learning shows as behavior that can be observed and measured. So write goals that way. “Before discharge, the client will demonstrate the device steps without prompting” is observable. “The client will understand the device” gives you nothing to check.

Effective teaching sets realistic goals that help the learner meet objectives. Include the client in setting goals. Choose objectives across all three domains when needed.

If a physical limit prevents the task, the goal may involve a trained caregiver or adapted equipment. Teach survival skills first, and reinforce the rest later.

rows: Explain the agreed schedule and what to do for a named concern, before discharge.
Demonstrate the steps using the actual device.
Describe the chosen plan and name one barrier with a practical response.
Select one relevant action, how often, and a review date.

sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 3, 9, 13, and 24

sections.heading: How do teach-back and return demonstration work?
sections.keyIdea: Teach a small piece, have the client explain or show it, and reteach any gap differently.
sections.body:
Go from simple to complex, and connect new ideas to what the client knows. Explain why each step matters. Let the client practice. Give specific, timely, nonjudgmental feedback.

Your course’s social learning theory says to model a skill, then ask for repeat demonstrations until performance is satisfactory. This is return demonstration. Watch the client perform with real or training equipment.

Teach-back is added from current practice. Frame it as a check on yourself: “I want to make sure I explained this clearly. Tell me how you will do this at home.” Ask for their own words, not a repeated phrase.
steps: Explain a small amount in plain language.
Ask the client to explain or demonstrate, without blame.
Notice what is correct and what is missing.
Reteach the gap with different words or a different method.
Check again, and plan reinforcement.
sections.example: During teach-back, a client says, “If I miss a dose, I will take two the next morning.” The written plan says otherwise. The nurse reteaches that one point a different way and checks again.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 15 and 18; teach-back added from AHRQ Teach-Back Method (Tool 5)

sections.heading: Compliance, adherence, and the “noncompliant” label
sections.keyIdea: Do not quickly label a client noncompliant. First find out why the plan is not being followed.
sections.body:
Your course defines two terms. Compliance is the extent to which a person’s behavior coincides with medical or health advice. It is best shown when the person accepts the need to learn and then follows through with actions.

Adherence is attachment to a prescribed regimen. It encourages patients to be committed, active participants in their own health. In mutual agreement, the patient plays an active role in choosing the course of treatment.

Do not quickly label a patient noncompliant. First find out why they are not following the plan. Nurses cannot control patients’ responses or change their habits. Common barriers are listed below.
bullets: Cost or insurance problems.
Side effects.
Misunderstanding.
Beliefs and values.
Limited support or trouble using supplies.
Competing responsibilities, such as work or caregiving.
sections.example: A client has not taken a blood pressure pill for a week. Staff call the client “noncompliant.” The client says, “Those pills make me dizzy when I stand up at work.” The nurse explores this side effect and involves the provider.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 10 and 22; barrier list added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: How do I document and plan for discharge?
sections.keyIdea: Evaluate the teaching, reinforce as needed, and document it. Speak up before discharge if an essential skill is not verified.
sections.body:
Your course ends every lifespan teaching plan the same way: evaluate the effectiveness of teaching, reinforce as needed, and document the teaching.

Record the learner, need, content, method, readiness, and language support. Say exactly what the client explained or demonstrated, and how much help they needed. “Understands” with no evidence does not guide the next nurse.

Include follow-up practice, referrals, and unsolved resource barriers. If essential learning has not happened, tell the team before discharge or transfer. One success may still need reinforcement over time.
sections.example: A client with a new colostomy is to be discharged in 1 hour. The client still needs step-by-step help to change the pouch, lives alone, and the first home health visit is in 3 days. The nurse notifies the provider and case manager about the unmet essential skill.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 20–21 and 24; discharge escalation added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Wrong answers repeat the same teaching, trust a nod, or label the client instead of finding the barrier.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: Wanting to learn does not help if pain or nausea blocks focus.
Teach-back checks your explanation. It is framed without blame.
A yes is not evidence. The client’s own explanation is.
Can explain but cannot open supplies? Adapt equipment or get help.
Do not label quickly. Missed doses may come from cost or side effects. Ask why.
Reteaching changes the words, method, pace, or support.
Family can support. A qualified interpreter handles teaching.
Charting an attempt does not fix an unmet essential skill.

sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials (reviews slides 10 and 18–19)

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Pick the answer that finds the barrier first, then teaches and verifies to match it.
sections.body:
Expect “what should the nurse do first” items about readiness or barriers. Others ask for the most observable objective. Select-all items test teach-back steps and assessment data.

Sample question: A client accurately explains a medication schedule but has missed refills. The client says the copayment is unaffordable. What should the nurse do first?

A: Reteach the medication schedule.
B: Explain the risks of missed doses.
C: Explore cost options with the client and the team, such as social work or pharmacy help.
D: Document the client as noncompliant.
steps: Read the stem: knowledge is correct, but refills are missed because of cost.
What is it really asking? What is the real barrier, and what fixes it?
Key cues: “accurately explains” rules out a knowledge gap. “Unaffordable” names the barrier.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A and B add teaching the client does not need. D labels instead of helping.
The answer: C. It matches the action to the cost barrier.
Strategy: Before choosing “teach,” ask whether the stem shows a knowledge gap at all.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials

sections.heading: Worked case: reteaching should change something
sections.keyIdea: If teaching did not work, change the method, not just the speed or volume.
sections.body:
A client repeats the first two steps of a care routine correctly. But the client leaves out the final safety check.

The nurse repeats the whole explanation three times, faster each time, and asks, “Do you understand now?” The client nods.

The nod does not show the gap is fixed. Repeating the same words faster is not reteaching.
steps: Name the exact missing step and why it matters.
Check for contributors: pain, fatigue, language, vision or hearing, memory load, or unclear wording.
Reteach just that part with clearer words or a demonstration.
Let the client practice, then ask them to show the whole sequence.
Give accurate feedback on what was right and what was missing.
If hand strength or supplies block success, adapt the plan instead of adding more words.
Document what the client did, prompts needed, changes after reteaching, and follow-up.

check.q: What should change after an unsuccessful teaching attempt?
check.a: Reassess the barrier, then adapt the content, method, pace, timing, access, or support. Repeating the same material faster is not a real change.

sections.source: Added: worked example based on Teaching and Learning slides 12, 18–19

sections.keyIdea: This topic follows Module 41 slides 3, 9–10, 13, 15, and 18–25. The notes below mark what the site adds.
sections.body: This lesson follows your Module 41 slides, “The Concept of Teaching and Learning.”
bullets: Learning need, compliance, and adherence: slide 10.
Factors that help or block learning: slides 18–19.
Measurable goals: slides 3, 9, 13, and 24. Return demonstration: slide 15.
Evaluate, reinforce, and document: slides 20–24. Home and support assessment: slide 25.
Added from current practice: teach-back, from the AHRQ Teach-Back Method, Tool 5 (ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/tool5.html); checked October 27, 2026.
Added from current practice: universal plain language and qualified interpreters. Added for the NCLEX: discharge escalation, traps, sample question, and worked case.

pearls: Assess the cause of difficulty before changing the teaching.
Readiness, motivation, understanding, physical ability, and access are separate.
Teach-back checks the explanation. Return demonstration checks the skill.
The most observable objective names a specific action and a time to check it.
Record the client’s actual response and the needs that remain.
redFlags: Unverified essential skills or missing supplies may make discharge unsafe.
Severe pain, acute confusion, or heavy sedation may block meaningful teaching and needs assessment.
A client who lives alone with an unmet essential skill needs team notification before discharge.

checks.a: As a check that the nurse explained clearly. Ask the client to explain the plan in their own words.

checks.q: A client knows the steps but cannot open supplies. What is the issue?
checks.a: A functional barrier. It needs adaptation or help, not more verbal explanation.

checks.q: What should happen after an incorrect return demonstration?
checks.a: Find the exact gap, reteach without judgment, allow practice, and check again.

checks.q: Why ask about cost after a missed medication refill?
checks.a: The barrier may be access, not understanding or motivation. The intervention must match it.

checks.q: A client will give daily injections at home. What should you assess first?
checks.a: Current knowledge, vision and hand ability, language, readiness, and resources such as supplies, storage, and cost.

topics.title: Lifespan Teaching, Caregivers & Online Health Information
topics.summary: Adapt teaching to development and function, involve caregivers wisely, and help clients judge and use online health information.
objectives: You can adapt teaching for children, adolescents, adults, and older adults.
You can verify the caregiver who will actually give care, without leaving out the client.
You can check that the home setup supports the plan.
You can judge online information by author, evidence, date, purpose, and fit.
You can assess digital access and offer usable alternatives.
topics.bigPicture:
The same information may need very different teaching for a child, a teen, a tired adult, or an older adult with poor vision. Age gives context. But development, function, language, experience, and the home setting shape the plan.

Videos, portals, and apps can extend learning. But a link does not guarantee access or quality. The nurse helps the learner find reliable information and checks that the tool works for them. Sometimes printed or in-person teaching is the better choice.
recap: Teach to development and function, not to age alone.
Assess the child’s development. Teach the caregiver, but include the child at their level, using props when appropriate.
Engage the teen directly. A parent’s agreement is not the teen’s learning.
For older adults, address aging factors, allow time and repetition, and include them in setting goals.
Watching is not doing. Verify the person who will actually give care at home.
Check that home help, supplies, and setup really exist before discharge.
Judge websites by author credentials, sponsor, references, and a current date. Wiki-type sites are not quality references.
Portals are for routine needs. Urgent symptoms need direct, immediate action.

keyTerms.def: Matching content, words, participation, and practice to what the person can actually do at their stage of development.
The support person’s willingness, understanding, ability, and resources to help safely.
Having a working device, internet connection, accessible format, language, and the skills to use them.
How trustworthy information is, based on the author’s expertise, evidence, openness, and purpose.
A personal or business gain, such as selling a product, that may bias how information is presented.
A hospital or clinic system that lets nurses and providers print personalized teaching materials. Patient portals for routine messages are not for emergencies.
Planned review and practice over time that helps the learner remember and use information correctly.
The movement to make healthcare resources more accessible to patients by moving them to electronic media.

sections.heading: How do I teach children?
sections.keyIdea: Assess the child’s development first. Direct teaching mainly to the parent or caregiver, but always include the child at their level.
sections.body:
First assess the child’s developmental level. Teaching for children usually focuses on primary healthcare, health promotion, and illness and injury prevention.

Direct the teaching plan mainly to the parent or primary caregiver. But you must also include the child. Give basic instructions at the child’s level.

Caregivers often do the essential care. They need their own explanation, practice, and evaluation. A parent watching a demonstration does not prove they can do it.

Your course’s steps for teaching a child:
sections.example: A 4-year-old will get nebulizer treatments with a face mask at home. The nurse has the child put the mask on a toy first, using short, concrete words. The parent also gets separate teaching, practice, and evaluation.
bullets: Build trust by calling the child by name.
Teach in a safe setting with a calm approach.
Allow time for questions and practice.
When appropriate, use props to demonstrate procedures.
Give feedback, praise, and encouragement.
Evaluate how well the teaching worked, and reinforce as needed.
Document the teaching.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 20

sections.heading: How do I teach adolescents?
sections.keyIdea: Assess the teen’s development and independence, respect their fears and feelings, and involve them directly to build trust.
sections.body:
Assess the teen’s developmental level and independence from parents or caregivers. Acknowledge and respect the teen’s fears and feelings. Aim for a calm environment.

Involve the teen in the teaching. This builds a trusting nurse–patient relationship, which your course calls essential for success. A parent’s agreement does not show the teen understands or is committed.

Focus teaching on safety, consequences, and personal responsibility. Teens face environmental influences, peer pressure, and risk-taking behavior. Allow time for questions and practice, and give feedback, praise, and encouragement. Evaluate, reinforce as needed, and document.

E-health tools may be especially helpful for teens. Not every teen has a private, reliable device, so ask first. Explaining privacy limits accurately is added from current practice.
sections.example: A 15-year-old with new type 1 diabetes sits silently while a parent answers. The teen rolls their eyes and looks at a phone. First, the nurse asks the teen what they already know and what worries them most. Scare tactics often make teens more defensive.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 21 and 28

sections.heading: How do I teach adults?
sections.keyIdea: Find each adult’s own learning preferences, every time. Your goal is knowledge and awareness. You cannot control their choices.
sections.body:
Seek each adult’s unique learning preferences. Do this even if you have worked with this patient before. Gather subjective and objective data, as listed below.

Knowing your own learning style may help you build teaching plans. Allow time for questions and practice. Give feedback, reassurance, and support. Stress the importance of positive health practices. Actively involve patients in their care.

Remember that nurses cannot control patients’ responses or change their habits. Your primary goals are providing knowledge and awareness. A client who chooses differently is not automatically uninformed. Explore their reasons, explain risks and options, and plan something feasible.
bullets: Personal demands and responsibilities.
Education level and cultural influences.
Motivation to learn.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 22

sections.heading: How do I teach older adults?
sections.keyIdea: Address aging factors that affect learning, give time and repetition, and include the older adult in planning and goal setting.
sections.body:
For older adults, teaching about chronic illness is essential for symptom control and prevention. Teaching plans center on nutrition, physical activity, personal safety, medication, and follow-up appointments.

Address aging factors that affect understanding, so the most learning can occur. The factors your course lists are below. Many older adults learn well once these are addressed.

Include the patient in building the plan and setting goals. Allow enough time to process information, and repeat key points. Include significant others or primary caregivers. Including them does not replace teaching the older adult. Use a calm approach in a peaceful setting. Evaluate, reinforce, and document.
bullets: Sensory changes (vision, hearing) and energy level.
Physical abilities, such as hand strength.
Cultural influences.
Memory, response time, and stress.
sections.example: An alert 82-year-old with arthritis in both hands is learning a new inhaler. She says, “I want to keep managing my own medicines.” Her son says, “Just teach me. She is too old to learn this.” First, the nurse assesses her grip on the inhaler and asks how she wants her son involved.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 23–24

sections.heading: Will the plan work at home?
sections.keyIdea: Before teaching, assess the home environment, support system, and developmental level. Each client’s needs shape the plan.
sections.body:
Each patient’s individual needs should shape the teaching plan. One client may have a mobility or cognitive impairment. Another may have an illness affected by their environment.

Before planning individual teaching, do a complete assessment of the home environment, the support system, and the developmental level. During teaching, you may need to stress the importance of interprofessional help to meet the client’s needs.

A skill may depend on a countertop, clean water, storage, or another person. Ask what the home actually offers. Teach with the real supplies whenever possible.
sections.example: A client with left-sided weakness after a stroke needs a two-handed dressing change daily. The only trained helper, a neighbor, will be away for 2 weeks. The nurse addresses this first, for example by arranging home health, training another helper, or adapting the method.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 25

sections.heading: How do I judge online health information?
sections.keyIdea: Check the author’s credentials, who sponsors the site, its references, and a current posting date. Wiki-type sites are not quality references.
sections.body:
Your course’s steps for judging a health website are listed below. The table sums them up as five questions.

Commercial sponsorship calls for caution. It does not prove every claim is false. A polished page or a recent date alone does not prove reliability.

Added for the NCLEX: warning signs include guaranteed cures, pressure to buy, and advice to stop prescribed treatment. Invite the client to share questionable pages without embarrassment. Shaming makes future sharing less likely.

rows: Sales or sponsorship can bias content.
Relevance to the actual care plan.

bullets: Consider the author’s credentials. Is it a personal website or one sponsored by an organization?
Review any “About Us,” “Philosophy,” or “Background” links.
Look for citations or references, with footnotes and working links. They should be reliable and high quality.
Check the publication or posting date on the page. It should be current.
Vet organizational websites carefully, too.
View sites of private companies promoting medical products with caution.
Popular nonscientific or “wiki” websites are not quality references.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 26–27; warning signs added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: How do I choose usable technology?
sections.keyIdea: E-health tools can personalize and reinforce teaching. They only help if the learner can access, understand, and use them.
sections.body:
Your course calls the shift of healthcare resources to electronic media the e-health movement. Its focus is making resources more accessible to patients. Technology gives nurses new ways to teach.

Before relying on a tool, assess internet, device, language, accessibility, privacy, and confidence. Show the real login steps and have the client show you. Offer print or in-person follow-up when needed.

Added for the NCLEX: teach which concerns need immediate direct contact and which can wait. Portal messages are for routine needs.
sections.example: After a cardiac procedure, a client says, “If my chest pain comes back tonight, I will send a portal message.” This needs more teaching. Returning chest pain needs the immediate direct action the client was taught, such as calling emergency services.
bullets: E-health portals let nurses and providers print teaching materials personalized for each patient.
Some facilities have smart TVs for videos and health learning apps.
Apps may include tutorials and quizzes that reinforce learning.
HIPAA-compliant video conferencing can be used for individualized teaching.
E-health may be especially helpful with adolescents.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 27–28; access checks and urgent-symptom teaching added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Wrong answers assume by age, trust a link or a watched video, or judge a website by its looks.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: Older age vs. inability to learn
Assess function. Adapt for vision, hands, or pace.
Watching is not doing. Have the caregiver practice and demonstrate.
Ask the teen directly what they know and worry about.
Confirm device, internet, language, and login before relying on it.
Check credentials, sponsor, references, and a current date.
A good source can still use the wrong product, language, or format.
Portals are for routine needs. Urgent symptoms need direct action.
Trained helper on paper vs. at home
Confirm the helper will actually be there.

sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials (reviews slides 20–28)

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Choose the answer that includes the learner, verifies the real caregiver, and fits real access.
sections.body:
Expect lifespan items about a child, teen, or older adult with a family member present. Select-all items often ask for website warning signs or what to check before using a video.

Sample question: A parent will do a child’s home care. The parent watched the demonstration but has not practiced, and discharge is near. What should the nurse do first?

A: Give a video link to review at home.
B: Have the parent perform the care while the nurse observes.
C: Document that teaching was completed.
D: Repeat the demonstration for the parent.
steps: Read the stem: the parent is the real caregiver, has only watched, and time is short.
What is it really asking? What evidence shows the caregiver can safely do the care?
Key cues: “watched” and “has not practiced” mean learning is not verified.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A and D give more watching, not doing. C records teaching, not learning.
The answer: B. A return demonstration verifies the person who will actually give care.
Strategy: Ask, “Who will do this at home, and have I seen them do it?”
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials

sections.heading: Worked case: a link does not create access
sections.keyIdea: When a resource does not work for the learner, change the resource, not your view of the learner.
sections.body:
A caregiver agrees to watch a home-care video. Later, the caregiver says the phone has limited data and the video is in an unfamiliar language. The supplies shown also differ from the ones at home.

This does not mean the caregiver refused or lacks motivation. Even a credible video may show another product or an outdated process.
steps: Assess technology, language, supplies, and who will actually give care.
Choose a credible resource that matches the real task and supplies.
Provide an accessible explanation in the caregiver’s language, with a qualified interpreter if needed.
Demonstrate with the correct supplies, then watch the caregiver practice.
Include the child or dependent client in a way that fits their development.
Ask how the routine will work at home. Confirm supplies and follow-up.
Document the adapted method and pass on remaining needs.

check.q: Can a credible resource still be unsuitable?
check.a: Yes. It may be inaccessible, in another language, show a different product, or not fit the client’s condition and home plan. Credibility and fit both matter.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.keyIdea: This topic follows Module 41 slides 20–28. The notes below mark what the site adds.
sections.body: This lesson follows your Module 41 slides, “The Concept of Teaching and Learning.”
bullets: Children, adolescents, adults, and older adults: slides 20–24.
Individual needs, home, and support assessment: slide 25.
Judging online health information: slides 26–27.
E-health, portals, apps, and video conferencing: slides 27–28.
Added for the NCLEX: website warning signs (guaranteed cures, sales pressure), digital access checks, and portal vs. emergency teaching.
Added from current practice: qualified interpreters and explaining a teen’s privacy limits within policy and law.
sections.source: Teaching and Learning slides 20–28 (map of this topic)

pearls: Teach to developmental and functional ability, not age alone.
Caregiver presence is not evidence of caregiver competence.
A credible website still must be relevant and current.
Digital tools need an access plan and verified learning.
When family speaks for an alert client, assess the client’s ability and ask how they want family involved.
redFlags: A website advising the client to stop prescribed treatment needs critical review with the care team.
Missing device access, essential supplies, or trained support can make a discharge plan unsafe.
Urgent symptoms need the instructed direct clinical response, not a routine portal message.

checks.q: Should all teaching for an older adult go to family?
checks.a: No. Assess the client’s abilities and wishes, and include supports as the client prefers.

checks.q: What should be checked before relying on a portal video?
checks.a: Device and internet access, language, sensory access, ability to use it, privacy, fit with real supplies, and actual learning afterward.

checks.q: Does a recent date prove online information is reliable?
checks.a: No. Also check author expertise, evidence, purpose, conflicts of interest, and relevance.

checks.q: A caregiver will do home care. What evidence is needed?
checks.a: The caregiver’s own explanation and demonstrated skill, plus feasible resources and a follow-up plan.

checks.q: A client brings a slick website selling its own “guaranteed cure” with no references. Best response?
checks.a: Without shaming, review the warning signs together: a guaranteed cure, a sales motive, and no evidence. Then discuss reliable sources.
